title: Two and a Half Letters
hookLine: a weaver's two-line answer to a shelf of books
carry: bhakti: love, not books, makes the pandit
tomorrow: Why does a deer search the forest for a scent it carries?

cards: A shelf sags under the weight of books, commentaries on commentaries. A scholar has spent his life there, and he can quote line and verse on anything you ask.

Down the lane, a weaver throws the shuttle back and forth at his loom. Tradition says he never learned to read. He has a two-line answer for the man with the shelf, about how much reading it takes to become wise.

teach.b: Today's doha begins, in Hindi, pothi padh padh jag mua.
A pothi is a book, a sacred text, and the line says, roughly: reading book after book, the whole world died, and not one became a pandit, a truly learned one.

Then the second line: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit. Two and a half letters is the doha's own count, and one common reading makes it a joke you can see on the page.
The Hindi word for love, prem, is written with a half letter joined to the front of a full one, and then one more. Kabir doesn't say books are bad; his own verses ended up in books.
He says something narrower and sharper: reading alone doesn't finish anyone. This is the heart of bhakti, the path of devotion all this week's saints walked.
In their teaching, God is reached by prem, love, and love can't be finished on paper. A grandmother who sings to Ram with her whole heart may have read more of it than the man with the shelf.
And here's the trap, like yesterday's. Some readers stop at the first line, pleased: ha, all those books. But the second line asks something of them too.
Have you read the two and a half letters? Not heard of them. Read them.
In Kabir's picture, love of God is the text, every day is the exam, and the exam isn't on paper.

how: This doha of Kabir is quoted in Hindi homes and classrooms as a saying about love and learning, and is sung in devotional settings by those who keep Kabir's songs.

o: a scholar who spent his life reading commentaries
a temple priest who taught the Veda in Kashi
the weaver-poet who said love is the real lesson

s: Kabir says reading book after book makes you a pandit
the world died reading, and not one became a pandit.
the two and a half letters are the word for love
prem is written with a half letter joined to a full one, then one more.
the doha says all books are bad
it says reading alone doesn't make anyone wise; love has to be read too.

games.q: you want to become truly wise, a pandit. a scholar shows you his shelf of books. a weaver gives you two and a half letters. what does Kabir's doha say to study?
o: every book on the shelf, one by one.
the two and a half letters of love.
nothing at all; wisdom can't be learned.
games.why: whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit, says the doha; the world died reading books without it.

practice: Choose one name of God you love: Ram, Krishna, Shiva, Ma, or the one your family uses. Say or sing it slowly three times, not as a lesson, but the way you'd say the name of someone you love.
That's the bhakti way of reading the two and a half letters. If you don't pray, say the name of someone you love the same way, and notice what changes in your voice.

wordCard.voice: Kabir. The weaver-poet of Kashi. Today's doha: reading book after book, no one became wise; whoever reads the two and a half letters of love becomes the pandit.

orig.note: Hindi, in Devanagari: love, the word Kabir counts as two and a half letters.
